pe135_creighton_address_1957.title: D. G. Creighton, “Presidential Address,” Report of the Annual Meeting of the Canadian Historical Association 36, no. 1 (1957): 1–12.
pe135_creighton_address_1957.citation: D. G. Creighton, “Presidential Address,” Report of the Annual Meeting / Rapports annuels de la Société historique du Canada 36, no. 1 (1957): 1–12. doi:10.7202/300399ar.

verification.note: Read in full (pp. 1–12) from page images of the Érudit PDF, via the Internet Archive capture of 20 November 2022; OCR checked against running heads. Quoted: 'In the 1930's, when the influence of Harold Innis was at its height and everybody was writing and talking about staple production' (p. 3); 'the Liberal Interpretation — or Authorized Version — of Canadian history' begun by Willison and Dafoe (p. 4); historians 'accepted, for historical purposes, the two highly fashionable political theories', 'the Marxian doctrine of the class struggle' and 'the Frontier Theory' (p. 6); the Marxian interpretation 'alien to their experience and unremunerative for their purposes'; Innis 'refused to accept the simplified Marxian version of historical determinism' (p. 6); the LSR claim about 'an economic empire for the entrepreneurs of Montreal' (pp. 6–7); 'a sadly imperfect vehicle for the exemplification of the Marxian verities' (p. 7); Turner 'fixed upon the movement of settlement across the continent as the most important fact in its history' (p. 8); frontier progress 'modified by ... railways, efficient police, governmental supervision', the 1837 rebels 'not from the frontier', 'forest-born' (p. 9); 'How wrong we were!' (p. 11); 'imported intellectual reach-me-downs' and 'less deference for imported theories of historical change' (p. 12).

pe135_creighton_address_1957.scope_note: In-period statement of his case against the Liberal, Marxian and frontier interpretations of Canadian history.

pe135_creighton_decline_1969.title: D. G. Creighton, “The Decline and Fall of the Empire of the St. Lawrence,” Historical Papers / Communications historiques 4, no. 1 (1969): 14–25.
pe135_creighton_decline_1969.citation: D. G. Creighton, “The Decline and Fall of the Empire of the St. Lawrence,” Historical Papers / Communications historiques (Canadian Historical Association) 4, no. 1 (1969): 14–25. doi:10.7202/030704ar.

verification.note: Read in full (pp. 14–25) from page images of the Érudit PDF, via the Internet Archive capture of 25 July 2024 (the live Érudit site returned a bot-check page); OCR checked against the page order and running heads. Quoted: the phrase 'made its first public appearance in the autumn of 1937' (he names the book The Empire of the St. Lawrence, its 1956 title); regarded 'as the inspiration, at least in part, of a new school of Canadian historians and as the genesis of a new historical doctrine, the Laurentian interpretation of Canadian history'; 'no wish to disavow the parentage of an idea'; the book as 'the fruit of my friendship with Harold Innis' called a simple generalization that 'happen[s] to be wrong' (p. 14); subject suggested 'not by Harold Innis, whom I barely knew at the time, but by W. P. M. Kennedy'; the Chateau Clique merchants and 'Montreal's staple trades' (p. 15); 'reluctantly convinced by the weight of his own evidence'; 'The protagonist of the Empire of the St. Lawrence was the River itself'; Macdonald as 'the only satisfactory method of writing the second phase' and 'a trilogy on one theme'; 'This Laurentian theme ...' and 'a great territorial empire, both commercial and political, in the western interior' (p. 16); 'the east-west axis would be its backbone' (p. 17); Confederation 'not of a cultural compact between two cultural groups' (p. 18); the First World War as 'the great divide' (p. 19); Mackenzie King 'not so much a Canadian citizen as a citizen of North America' (p. 21); 'Canada now stands alone' and 'American economic and military imperialism' (p. 22); 'ethnic and cultural values' (p. 24); duality, bilingualism and a special position for Quebec 'a repudiation of the intentions of the Fathers of Confederation' (p. 25).

pe135_creighton_decline_1969.scope_note: The author's own retrospect on the Laurentian theme (1969) and his account of its 'decline and fall'; a later statement, not evidence of the 1937 text.
